questions.question: What is the most accurate description of pharmacogenomics?
choices: Study of how genetic variation can influence response to selected medications
A method that guarantees the correct medication for every patient
A replacement for medication reconciliation and monitoring
A test that diagnoses every cause of an adverse effect
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenomics can inform selected medication decisions, but drug response also depends on clinical, organ-function, interaction, and adherence factors.

questions.question: Why is a genotype result not automatically a prescription instruction?
choices: The result must be interpreted for the specific drug and integrated with phenotype, labeling, interactions, organ function, and clinical context
Genes never affect drug response
Every variant requires stopping all medications
A patient’s symptoms are irrelevant after genetic testing
questions.explanation: A genetic result is one component of a clinical decision. Its actionability depends on the exact drug-gene pair and the patient’s full situation.

questions.question: What does phenoconversion describe?
choices: Non-genetic factors such as drug interactions or organ dysfunction changing real-world metabolic activity despite a stable genotype
A laboratory changing a patient’s DNA
A patient forgetting a medication name
A genetic result becoming permanently invalid
questions.explanation: Interactions, illness, and organ dysfunction can change functional drug metabolism. Medication reconciliation remains essential even when genotype is known.

questions.question: When is pharmacogenomic testing most likely to be useful?
choices: When a validated, actionable result could change a timely medication decision
For every routine prescription regardless of evidence
Only after a patient stops all medications
When no clinical question has been defined
questions.explanation: Testing has the greatest value when the result is reliable, relevant to the drug, available in time, and tied to a meaningful management action.

questions.question: A patient brings a direct-to-consumer genetic report and wants to stop an essential medication today. What is the best FNP response?
choices: Review the exact report and medication, explain limitations, assess clinical safety, and obtain confirmation or expert input if the result could change care
Tell the patient to stop immediately without review
Ignore the patient’s concern because consumer tests are never meaningful
Promise that the report proves the medication is harmful
questions.explanation: Direct-to-consumer reports vary in tested variants and clinical evidence. Do not make abrupt high-stakes changes without appropriate interpretation and clinical assessment.

questions.question: Which resource should an FNP check for current medication-specific pharmacogenomic prescribing information?
choices: Current FDA-approved drug labeling and applicable evidence-based implementation guidance
A social-media post about genetic testing
A generic list of gene names without the drug context
An old class note used as the only source
questions.explanation: FDA labeling provides current prescribing and safety information. Evidence-based guidance may help interpret an available result for a specific drug-gene pair.

questions.question: A patient has unexpected medication toxicity and a relevant genetic variant, a new interacting drug, and worsening kidney function. What is the safest conclusion?
choices: Several factors may contribute, so assess the combined drug-gene, drug-drug, and organ-function problem
The genetic variant must be the only cause
Kidney function and interactions no longer matter
The adverse effect proves every future medication will fail
questions.explanation: Medication response is multifactorial. Genetic information should be integrated with interactions, dosing, organ function, illness, and the clinical presentation.

questions.question: Why should clinically actionable pharmacogenomic results be documented carefully?
choices: They may have durable relevance, but future clinicians need the source, interpretation, evidence, and decision rather than an oversimplified label
They should never be visible to future prescribers
A raw gene name alone explains all future prescriptions
Documentation removes the need for monitoring
questions.explanation: Careful documentation supports safe continuity. Interpretation can evolve, so the source, phenotype, evidence, plan, and follow-up matter.

questions.question: Which statement reflects an equity-focused pharmacogenomics practice?
choices: Use validated testing when indicated, explain panel limitations, and do not use race as a substitute for an individual genotype
Assume ancestry alone determines every drug response
Withhold treatment from patients without genetic testing
Assume every test panel detects every relevant variant equally
questions.explanation: Evidence and test coverage can vary. Ancestry categories are not a substitute for patient-specific validated testing and clinical evaluation.

questions.question: When should an FNP consider expert consultation for pharmacogenomics?
choices: When interpretation is complex, the medication is high risk, interactions are substantial, or the result conflicts with the clinical picture
Only when the patient has no symptoms
Never, because any genetic report is self-explanatory
Only after making an irreversible medication change
questions.explanation: Pharmacists with pharmacogenomics expertise, genetic counselors, specialists, and institutional services can help with complex or high-stakes decisions.
